title: Future and probability: what will happen, and how sure are you?
goal: Talk about the future the way Swedes do — choosing between *ska*, *kommer att*, *tänker* and the plain present — and say exactly how likely something is.
bekal: you can tell a plan (*ska*) from a prediction (*kommer att*) and a personal intention (*tänker*)
you can grade probability from *säkert* through *troligen* and *nog* down to *knappast*
you can use *lär* ("is bound to, is said to") and place sentence adverbs correctly in main and subordinate clauses
wave: Go back to Svenska 102, Unit 12: reread the dialogue and sort every future sentence into two piles — *ska* (somebody decided) and *kommer att* (nobody decided, it just happens). Then add a third pile for this unit: *tänker*.

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Planeringsmötet
dialogs.intro: Monday morning at the design agency in Göteborg. Karin, Dian's boss, has called the project team together: a client's new app has to be launched in December, and the schedule is tight. Mattias is the team's tester; Dian is drawing the screens.

lines.speaker: Karin:
lines.text: Okej, allihop. Vi ska lansera den nya appen den femtonde december.
lines.id: OK, everybody. We're launching the new app on the fifteenth of December.
lines.literal: okay, all-up. we shall launch the new app-the the fifteenth December.

lines.speaker: Mattias:
lines.text: Hinner vi verkligen det? Testerna kommer att ta minst tre veckor.
lines.id: Are we really going to make it? The testing will take at least three weeks.
lines.literal: make-it we really that? tests-the come to take at-least three weeks.

lines.speaker: Karin:
lines.text: Jag vet. Därför ska vi börja testa redan nästa måndag.
lines.id: I know. That's why we're starting the testing as early as next Monday.
lines.literal: I know. therefore shall we begin test already next Monday.

lines.speaker: Dian:
lines.text: Jag tänker göra klart skisserna till startsidan i helgen.
lines.id: I'm planning to finish the sketches for the home screen this weekend.
lines.literal: I think do finished sketches-the to start-page-the in weekend-the.

lines.speaker: Karin:
lines.text: Snällt, men du ska inte jobba i helgen. Det gör vi inte här.
lines.id: That's kind, but you're not to work this weekend. We don't do that here.
lines.literal: kind, but you shall not work in weekend-the. that do we not here.

lines.speaker: Dian:
lines.text: Okej. Då blir de antagligen klara på tisdag.
lines.id: OK. Then they'll probably be done on Tuesday.
lines.literal: okay. then become they presumably ready on Tuesday.

lines.speaker: Mattias:
lines.text: Kunden lär bli nöjd. De har väntat på den här appen i ett år.
lines.id: The client is bound to be happy. They've been waiting for this app for a year.
lines.literal: customer-the is-bound-to become satisfied. they have waited on the here app-the in a year.

lines.speaker: Karin:
lines.text: Förhoppningsvis. Men det kommer säkert att bli några ändringar i sista minuten.
lines.id: Hopefully. But there are sure to be a few last-minute changes.
lines.literal: hopefully. but it comes surely to become some changes in last minute-the.

lines.speaker: Mattias:
lines.text: Det blir det alltid.
lines.id: There always are.
lines.literal: it becomes it always.

lines.speaker: Karin:
lines.text: Precis. Dian, kommer du att kunna presentera skisserna för kunden?
lines.id: Exactly. Dian, will you be able to present the sketches to the client?
lines.literal: exactly. Dian, come you to be-able present sketches-the for customer-the?

lines.speaker: Dian:
lines.text: Jag tror det. Men min svenska kommer nog inte att vara perfekt.
lines.id: I think so. But my Swedish probably won't be perfect.
lines.literal: I believe it. but my Swedish comes probably not to be perfect.

lines.speaker: Karin:
lines.text: Den kommer att räcka gott. Och jag ska sitta bredvid dig hela tiden.
lines.id: It'll be more than enough. And I'll be sitting right next to you the whole time.
lines.literal: it comes to suffice well. and I shall sit beside you whole time-the.

notes: **Vi ska lansera** vs **testerna kommer att ta** — the two workhorses of the Swedish future side by side. *Ska* means somebody has **decided**: the launch date is Karin's plan. *Kommer att* is a **forecast**: nobody decides how long testing takes, it just will. A good test: if you can add "we've decided", use *ska*; if you can add "I predict", use *kommer att*.

**Jag tänker göra klart** — *tänka* + infinitive (no *att*) means "to intend to, to plan to". It is *your* private decision, so it sounds more personal than *ska*: *Jag tänker sluta röka* = I've made up my mind to quit smoking. *Göra klart* (**YÖ-rah KLAHT**) means "to finish" — literally "make ready".

**Du ska inte jobba i helgen** — *ska* can also carry an instruction or a firm piece of advice from someone else: "you're not to". Karin is being kind, but it is still an order. And *i helgen* is "this (coming) weekend" — the same *i* + definite form you met for *i fredags* (last Friday) in Svenska 102, but pointing forward.

**Kunden lär bli nöjd** — *lär* (**lehr**) is a small modal verb with a big job: "is bound to, is very likely to". It takes a bare infinitive, exists only in this one present-tense form, and has nothing to do with *lära* (to teach/learn) apart from the spelling. You will meet its second meaning in the next dialogue.

**Det kommer säkert att bli** — a sentence adverb such as *säkert*, *nog*, *inte* or *troligen* slips in **between** *kommer* and *att*: *det kommer **säkert** att bli*, *min svenska kommer **nog inte** att vara perfekt*. In everyday speech many Swedes drop *att* altogether (*det kommer bli bra*); in writing, keep it.

**Kommer du att kunna presentera?** — modal verbs like *kunna* have no future form of their own, so Swedish builds one: *kommer att kunna* = "will be able to", *kommer att behöva* = "will need to". English does exactly the same thing with "will be able to".

grammars.title: Four ways to talk about the future
body: English has *will*, *be going to* and *be -ing*; Swedish has four tools of its own. They overlap, but each has a home ground.

head: Form
Core meaning
Example
rows: a plan, decision or arrangement; also an order or a suggestion (*Ska vi…?*)
a fixed, near future — the most common of all in speech

after: The **present tense** is Swedish's default future as soon as a time expression makes the meaning clear: *Vi ses imorgon*, *Tåget går klockan sju*. Learners tend to overuse *ska* and *kommer att*; Swedes often need neither.

With **bli** (become) and weather or result verbs, the plain present already sounds like a prediction: *Det blir regn imorgon* = It's going to rain tomorrow. *Det kommer att bli regn* is correct too, just a little heavier.
The past **tänkte** is softer than *tänker*: *Jag tänkte fråga dig en sak* = I was going to ask you something / I thought I'd ask you something. It is one of the politest ways to open a request.

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Efter jobbet
dialogs.intro: Friday afternoon. Dian and her colleague Leila walk to the bus stop at Lindholmen after work. Oskar's parents have invited Dian to dinner, and Göteborg is doing what Göteborg does best: raining.

lines.speaker: Leila:
lines.text: Vad ska du göra i helgen, då?
lines.id: So what are you doing this weekend?
lines.literal: what shall you do in weekend-the, then?

lines.speaker: Dian:
lines.text: Oskars föräldrar har bjudit mig på middag igen, på lördag. Hemma hos dem i Askim.
lines.id: Oskar's parents have invited me to dinner again, on Saturday. At their place in Askim.
lines.literal: Oskar's parents have invited me on dinner again, on Saturday. home at them in Askim.

lines.speaker: Leila:
lines.text: Vad trevligt! Tänker du ta med något?
lines.id: How nice! Are you thinking of bringing something?
lines.literal: what nice! think you take with something?

lines.speaker: Dian:
lines.text: Jag tänkte köpa blommor, eller kanske en flaska vin.
lines.id: I was thinking of buying flowers, or maybe a bottle of wine.
lines.literal: I thought buy flowers, or maybe a bottle wine.

lines.speaker: Leila:
lines.text: Blommor är alltid säkert. Och ta med paraply — det lär regna hela helgen.
lines.id: Flowers are always safe. And bring an umbrella — it's supposed to rain all weekend.
lines.literal: flowers is always safe. and take with umbrella — it is-said-to rain whole weekend-the.

lines.speaker: Dian:
lines.text: Igen? Det har ju regnat nästan varje dag sedan jag kom hit.
lines.id: Again? It's rained almost every day since I got here.
lines.literal: again? it has you-know rained almost every day since I came here.

lines.speaker: Leila:
lines.text: Välkommen till Göteborg! Men på söndag blir det troligen sol.
lines.id: Welcome to Göteborg! But on Sunday it'll probably be sunny.
lines.literal: welcome to Göteborg! but on Sunday becomes it probably sun.

lines.speaker: Dian:
lines.text: Då tänker jag ta färjan ut i skärgården igen.
lines.id: Then I'm planning to take the ferry out to the archipelago again.
lines.literal: then think I take ferry-the out in archipelago-the again.

lines.speaker: Leila:
lines.text: Gör det! Färjorna går från Saltholmen. Du kommer att älska Vrångö.
lines.id: Do it! The ferries leave from Saltholmen. You're going to love Vrångö.
lines.literal: do it! ferries-the go from Saltholmen. you come to love Vrångö.

lines.speaker: Dian:
lines.text: Följer du med?
lines.id: Will you come along?
lines.literal: follow you with?

lines.speaker: Leila:
lines.text: Kanske. Jag ska hjälpa min syster att flytta på lördag, så jag är antagligen helt slut på söndag.
lines.id: Maybe. I'm helping my sister move on Saturday, so I'll probably be completely worn out on Sunday.
lines.literal: maybe. I shall help my sister to move on Saturday, so I am presumably totally finished on Sunday.

lines.speaker: Dian:
lines.text: Jag förstår. Skicka ett sms om du orkar.
lines.id: I understand. Text me if you feel up to it.
lines.literal: I understand. send a text if you have-the-energy.

notes: **Jag tänkte köpa blommor** — the past tense *tänkte* here does not mean that Dian *thought* something in the past; it means "I was thinking of, I had in mind to". It leaves the door open, which is why Swedes use it to sound tentative: *Jag tänkte gå hem nu* = I think I'll head home now.

**Det lär regna hela helgen** — the second meaning of *lär*: "it is said that, reportedly". Leila has seen the forecast, so *lär* passes on information from somewhere else. Context decides between "is bound to" and "is said to"; often both fit, as here.

**Troligen** (**TROO-li-gen**) and **antagligen** (**ahn-TAHG-li-gen**) both mean "probably" and can be swapped almost everywhere. They are sentence adverbs, so they follow the verb-second rule: *på söndag blir det **troligen** sol* — but in a subordinate clause they move in front of the verb, just like *inte*: *…eftersom det **troligen** blir sol*.

**Skärgården** (**HWEHR-goh-den**) — the archipelago. Göteborg's southern islands, such as Styrsö (**STÜSH-ö**) and Vrångö, are car-free and reached by the city's ordinary public-transport ferries from Saltholmen. Your bus card works on the boat.

**Jag ska hjälpa min syster att flytta** — *ska* for an arrangement already made. You will also hear *hjälpa min syster flytta* and *hjälpa min syster med flytten*; all three are fine. And **helt slut** (**helt slüt**) — literally "completely finished" — is the everyday way to say "exhausted".

**Om du orkar** — *orka* (**OR-kah**) means "to have the energy or strength to". There is no single English verb for it: *Jag orkar inte* = I can't be bothered / I'm too tired. Together with *hinna* (to have time to), it is one of the two most Swedish verbs you can own.

grammars.title: How sure are you? A probability scale
body: Swedish grades certainty with sentence adverbs. Learn them as a ladder, from top to bottom:

head: Adverb
Certainty
Example
rows: Vi hinner **knappast** bli klara till december.

after: Careful with **säkert**: on its own it often means only "surely, I bet" and is weaker than English "certainly". *Han är säkert hemma* = He's probably home, I'd bet. To say "definitely", use *definitivt* or *garanterat*.

**Kanske** is the one adverb that happily stands first without causing inversion in casual speech: *Kanske jag följer med* is common, though *Kanske följer jag med* is the textbook version and always correct.
**Lär** expresses probability with a verb instead of an adverb: *Det lär regna* ≈ *Det regnar troligen*. It cannot stand in the past or the perfect — for those, switch to an adverb.

sections.title: Plans, predictions and where the adverb goes

blocks.text: Choosing the future form is mostly about **who is in control**. If a person decides, it is *ska* or *tänker*; if the world decides, it is *kommer att*; if a time word does the work, the plain present is enough. The same event can take different forms depending on how you see it:

head: Sentence
What it tells you
rows: My decision, maybe not yet arranged.
It's going to happen (a prediction about my life).
Most likely / so I hear — rare about yourself, natural about others.

blocks.text: Sentence adverbs keep the positions you learned in Unit 3. In a **main clause** they come after the finite verb (and after the subject if it was pushed behind the verb); in a **subordinate clause** they come before the finite verb. With *kommer att* the finite verb is *kommer*, so the adverb stands right after it:

items: Hon **kommer troligen att** ringa. — main clause
Imorgon **kommer hon troligen att** ringa. — inverted main clause
…eftersom hon **troligen kommer att** ringa. — subordinate clause
Jag **ska nog inte** hinna. → …att jag **nog inte ska** hinna.

blocks.title: Ska is more than a future
items: **Suggestion:** *Ska vi ta en fika?* = Shall we grab a coffee?
**Order or rule:** *Du ska inte jobba i helgen.* / *Man ska ta av sig skorna.*
**What's expected:** *Hur ska jag veta det?* = How am I supposed to know?
**Destination without a verb of motion:** *Vart ska du?* — *Jag ska till jobbet.* The verb *gå/åka* is understood.

blocks.text: Swedish weather forecasts — from SMHI, the national weather service — are a perfect listening exercise for this unit, because they are nothing but predictions: *Under eftermiddagen **kommer** det **att** klarna upp. Imorgon **blir** det uppehåll i väster.* Notice how forecasters mix *kommer att* and *blir* freely.

Göteborg's weather is a running joke among Swedes: the city is said to have "two seasons, rain and almost rain". A local will often answer a complaint about the weather with a shrug and the classic *Det finns inget dåligt väder, bara dåliga kläder* — there's no bad weather, only bad clothes.

blocks.title: Spiral review — back to Unit 3
items: Take five sentences from this unit's dialogues and move a different element to the front each time: *Det blir troligen sol på söndag* → *På söndag blir det troligen sol* → *Troligen blir det sol på söndag.*
Check that the verb stays in second place and that *troligen* never lands in front of the verb in a main clause.
Then put each one after *Leila säger att…* and watch the adverb jump in front of the verb.
